title: STORM: Synergistic Cross-Scale Spatio-Temporal Modeling for Weather Forecasting
one_liner: Split weather patterns into separate models for each spatial and temporal scale, then combine them to forecast how the atmosphere evolves at all scales together.
lead: Weather happens at many scales at once: huge planetary wind patterns, regional storms, and tiny local gusts. Most weather models train one neural network on everything mixed together, which means they struggle to learn how each scale actually works. STORM separates the atmosphere into scale-specific patterns, learns what each one does independently, then ties them back together to make predictions.

problem.h2: Weather patterns hide inside mixed scales
paras: Weather happens because air moves and temperature shifts, but the reason it moves is different at each scale. A hurricane (scale: 1,000 km, timescale: days) forms because of sea-surface temperature gradients and planetary rotation. A thunderstorm (scale: 10 km, timescale: hours) forms because warm air rises fast enough to overcome Earth's gravity. A breeze (scale: 100 m, timescale: minutes) forms because the ground heats unevenly. All three happen at the same time, and a naive model — one neural network trained on raw gridded atmosphere data — must learn all three mechanisms at once, tangled together. Each scale's weights (the internal numbers the network uses to process data) end up capturing a blurry mixture.

What happens next is a beginner might hope that throwing more data or bigger networks at the raw mixture would help. It does not, because the network has no way to cleanly separate a hurricane pattern from a storm pattern when they arrive in the same input tensor (a table of numbers). The network's gradients (the directions to nudge the weights to fit the data) get pulled in conflicting directions — nudges that help the network recognize hurricanes hurt its ability to recognize storms, and vice versa, because a single set of weights cannot simultaneously capture both fast hurricane-scale and slow storm-scale dynamics cleanly. The result: the model learns poorly at all scales.

callout.html: STORM disentangles the atmosphere into separate scale-specific models, then combines their predictions so each scale learns cleanly.

steps.text: Break the atmospheric data into separate frequency bands: coarse grids capture planetary-scale patterns, fine grids capture local turbulence.
Train one neural network branch on each scale; each learns its own temporal dynamics without interference.
Each branch generates the next state of the atmosphere at its own scale and timescale independently.
Enforce consistency: coarse predictions must align with the average of fine predictions; no contradictions.
Combine predictions across scales into a single, coherent forecast at all resolutions from global to local.

paras: STORM changes how the input data is prepared before the neural network sees it. Instead of feeding raw atmospheric grids directly, it first separates them into multiple scale-specific decompositions — coarser grids for planetary patterns, finer grids for local details. Each decomposition is a different view of the same atmosphere, but at a different level of zoom.

hidden.name: per-scale learning consistency
paras: The hidden quantity STORM measures is the coherence — or mutual consistency — between predictions at different scales. When you predict the next atmospheric state, you are making estimates at coarse resolution (e.g., air pressure on a 200-km grid) and fine resolution (e.g., air pressure on a 25-km grid). If you naively average the coarse prediction, it should match the coarse version of the fine prediction, otherwise the scales contradict each other. Without enforcing this constraint, each scale-specific network learns independently and produces conflicting forecasts.

STORM estimates this quantity during training by comparing the predicted coarse field with the spatially averaged fine field. When they diverge, the loss (a penalty applied to the network) grows. The paper does not spell out a single formula but uses a multi-resolution consistency term to keep forecasts coherent.

heat.caption: Darker means stronger coherence; boundaries enforce consistency between scale predictions.

reads.html: Each scale-specific model learns to predict its own piece of the weather, but they must all agree when converted to the same resolution.
The framework maintains cross-resolution consistency via a multi-scale coherence loss that ensures coarse and fine predictions do not contradict.

mechanism.h2: Why breaking scales apart makes forecasts better
paras: The mechanism is simple: when a neural network learns from mixed-scale data, its weights end up capturing a blurred average of all scales, because the gradients (directions to improve) point in conflicting directions. A weight adjustment that helps it recognize a hurricane hurts its ability to recognize a breeze. By splitting the data into separate scales first, each scale-specific network receives cleaner input, so its gradients all point in coherent directions. A weight that recognizes fast-changing local convection never needs to unlearn hurricane-scale dynamics.

Then, when making predictions, STORM ties the scales back together with a coherence constraint. After each scale-specific branch generates its forecast, STORM checks: does the spatially-averaged fine-scale forecast match the coarse-scale forecast? If not, the loss penalizes the mismatch, steering both branches toward a unified answer. This constraint is the glue: it forces the scales to cooperate even though they learned separately. The result is that each scale captures its own true dynamics (hurricanes, storms, breezes) cleanly and independently, and then the coherence term ensures they combine into a single, self-consistent weather forecast.

stages.s: Decompose into coarse, medium, fine grids
Each branch learns its scale's dynamics independently
Generate per-scale predictions for next time step
Enforce coherence: coarse must match averaged fine

math.words: total loss equals scale-specific prediction errors plus a coherence penalty that grows when coarse predictions contradict spatially-averaged fine predictions.
symbols: prediction error for scale i (how far off the forecast is from true data)
the fine-scale forecast spatially averaged to coarse resolution
the forecast made at coarse resolution
how strongly to penalize scale mismatches
squared difference (a measure of distance between two numbers)

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose coarse grid predicts temperature 15C at a 200-km region.
Fine grid (25-km resolution) predicts 14C, 16C, 14C, 16C in the four 25-km cells.
If fine had predicted 12C, 18C, 14C, 16C instead, average = 15C still, so still 0 penalty.
If fine predicted 10C, 12C, 14C, 10C instead, average = 11.5C, then mismatch = (15-11.5)^2 = 12.25 (strong penalty, scales contradict).

math.note: The equation enforces that when you zoom out from the fine grid, you should see exactly what the coarse grid predicts.

charts.title: Naive single-network model
charts.note: One network tries to handle all scales at once; each scale suffers because weights blur together.

charts.title: STORM (scale-disentangled)
charts.note: Each scale-specific branch learns cleanly because it sees only its own scale, not tangled with others; the coherence constraint ties them together so they output consistent forecasts; all scales improve because conflicts between scales vanish.

items.html: If you break the atmosphere into too many scales, each branch gets too little data to learn from, and overfits (memorizes noise instead of learning patterns). There is a trade-off: more scales means more detail but also more numbers the network must tune.

If lambda (the strength of the coherence term) is too small, the scale-specific branches ignore the constraint and learn independently, producing contradictory forecasts. The forecast might predict a hurricane at coarse resolution but fine details that average to no hurricane.

If lambda is too large, the coherence term dominates, and the scale-specific branches sacrifice prediction accuracy to keep scales perfectly aligned. The result is a coherent but less accurate forecast.

Pick scale breakpoints that match real atmospheric boundaries (e.g., Rossby radius, boundary-layer height) and set lambda by cross-validation. The method works when decomposition captures real physics.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a tiny weather forecast experiment on a synthetic or small real dataset. Generate random multi-scale noise (e.g., large planetary sinusoids plus small local noise) as the training data. Train two models: (1) a baseline that takes all scales as input and predicts the next state, and (2) STORM that disentangles into two scales, trains separate branches, and enforces coherence. Measure prediction error at each scale separately and the overall forecast accuracy. Also measure how often the two scales contradict (e.g., coarse prediction versus averaged fine prediction). The demo should make it impossible to miss that STORM trades off between per-scale accuracy (depending on lambda) but keeps scale contradictions low.
demo.closing: STORM wins when scale-specific errors are lower than the baseline and scale contradictions are near zero.
